extracted.title: Cracking the Wall of Confinement: Understanding and Analyzing Malicious Domain Take-downs
extracted.venue: NDSS Symposium 2019 (peer reviewed), 24 to 27 February 2019; copy read from an author's university page
extracted.inclusion: included (Part A): domain takedown and sinkholing; outcome is the duration of the measure and release and re-registration of taken-down domains; method stated (sinkhole feeds, eight blacklists, passive DNS over about six years, historical WHOIS; registrar availability queried twice weekly October 2017 to May 2018)
extracted.data_public: no: commercial passive DNS (Farsight) and WHOIS from an industry collaborator
extracted.funder: US National Science Foundation grants, as stated
outcome_facts: "On average, malicious domains have been taken-down for two years" (Section I)

"350K domains (56.46%) of all the taken-down domains in the past six years have been released"; "7,148 (14.14%) of the domains taken down in the past ten months have been released back to the public registry domain pools" (Section V-A)
"4,418 domains were sinkholed more than once"; "340 domains seem to be re-registered domains, with an average release time of 237.5 days" (Section IV)
Of 133 domains active between two sinkholings by different parties, 28 had archived snapshots; authors "found two confirmed cases" of malicious reuse (Section V-B)
Sinkhole durations vary by the party taking the domain down; Discussion: one technology company "maintains an average take-down duration of three years, while registrars average one year"
extracted.safety_note: The paper also reports weaknesses in how some takedowns were administered; under the brief these are not restated, and no host, domain or operator detail is kept.
